strengths: Originality/significance: The paper identifies a real weakness of concept bottleneck models—supervised concept accuracy does not establish that a predictor uses the intended visual evidence—and proposes an intuitive combination of concepts, localized parts, and prototypes.

Soundness: The probabilistic formulation is mostly coherent, and the ELBO derivation clearly exposes the reconstruction, concept, task, and prototype-selection objectives. Re-encoding decoded prototypes and later replacing them with training image parts are sensible attempts to improve inspectability.

Presentation: The manuscript is generally clear and well organized. The concept-alignment table and qualitative examples communicate the intended model behavior effectively, and the capacity-versus-interpretability trade-off is acknowledged.

The experiments cover synthetic, controlled-scene, and real-face data. The noisy-label experiment provides preliminary evidence that prototype-level editing can improve concept accuracy, from about 92.8–92.9% to 96.9–97.8% on ColorMNIST+.

The authors report three seeds, computational hardware, an intervention policy, and several implementation choices, and they explicitly recognize that increasing the number of prototypes increases cognitive load.
weaknesses: Soundness: The central claim—human-verifiable concept alignment—is not convincingly evaluated. The evidence consists primarily of selected qualitative rows from seed 1; there is no user study, systematic prototype-alignment annotation, coverage/error analysis over all prototypes, or comparison of auditing accuracy and effort. Attractive examples cannot establish that humans can reliably discover misalignment, especially with 120 CelebA prototypes.

The intervention experiment is insufficiently specified and appears to rely on oracle knowledge of the injected label corruption. The paper does not state how erroneous prototypes were identified, how many were edited or removed, whether selection used validation or test information, or what human effort was required. Consequently, Table 3 does not validate the proposed human auditing workflow. The claim that such edits are impossible for standard CBMs is also too strong without comparisons to fine-tuning or model-editing baselines.

The accuracy claims are overstated. On CelebA, PGCM is materially worse than CBM in both concept accuracy (78.5% versus 81.3%) and task accuracy (83.0% versus 84.0%), with reported standard deviations much smaller than the gaps. CLEVR-Hans presents only a prototype-count curve and no baseline comparison. Thus the claimed matching of state-of-the-art CBMs is not generally demonstrated.

The intervention evaluation reports concept accuracy rather than downstream task accuracy. Accuracy necessarily improves when concepts are replaced with ground truth, so Figure 4 offers limited evidence of useful intervenability. PGCM* provides only a very small gain on ColorMNIST+ and is worse than ordinary intervention on CelebA.

Several claimed guarantees are not valid as stated. Re-encoding a generated prototype does not ensure that its embedding contains only human-visible semantic information because encoder/decoder networks can exploit imperceptible signals. Likewise, masking pixels does not guarantee that masked information was unused when the segmentation network observes the full image and mask shapes or boundaries can encode contextual information.

Important method details are ambiguous or inconsistent. Appendix A.2 describes a dot product between f_concept(e_j) and f_enc(x_i), which generally have concept-space and embedding-space dimensions, respectively. The aggregation of part-level concepts into the task input is not formally defined. Relabeling entries in a displayed table is not connected to a precise parameter-update or inference rule, and the procedures for adding prototypes and handling duplicates are not evaluated.

Reproducibility is inadequate for the reported results: there is no code or artifact availability statement, and the paper omits dataset sizes/splits, architecture widths and depths, batch size, epoch count, loss weights, fixed Gaussian variance, thresholding details, preprocessing, mask quality, editing criteria, and many dataset-specific settings. CLEVR-Hans additionally uses SAM with bounding-box prompts, potentially supplying privileged localization, without an analysis of segmentation dependence.

Significance is limited by strong supervision and localization requirements. CelebA uses semantic masks, ColorMNIST+ uses ground-truth digit masks, and CLEVR-Hans uses bounding-box prompts. There is no comparison against the closest locality-aware or concept-trustworthiness approaches, no segmentation ablation, and no evidence that the method remains useful with realistic imperfect localization.

Presentation and ethics: The paper lacks a dedicated limitations or broader-impact discussion. Using CelebA to predict subjective or sensitive attributes such as “Attractive,” “Male,” and “Young” warrants discussion of demographic bias, label validity, privacy, and harmful deployment. These concerns are especially relevant because the paper frames the resulting models as verifiable and trustworthy.

Combining part-level prototypes, explicit concept predictions, and prototype-level editing is a potentially useful design. The qualitative examples on CelebA, ColorMNIST+, and CLEVR-Hans illustrate the intended behavior clearly.

The evaluation includes several CBM baselines, three random seeds, a prototype-count study, intervention curves, and a controlled noisy-label experiment. The paper also supplies an ELBO derivation and a computational-complexity discussion.
The work acknowledges a real capacity-versus-cognitive-load tradeoff: increasing the number of prototypes improves accuracy but makes inspection harder.
weaknesses: The central claim—human-verifiable concept alignment—is not convincingly evaluated. Tables 1–2 contain a few selected examples from one seed, but there is no user study, exhaustive prototype audit, prototype-purity/alignment metric, evaluator agreement, time or error analysis, or experiment involving spurious visual correlations. Recognizable prototypes do not by themselves demonstrate that people can reliably verify the model at realistic scale (120 prototypes on CelebA).

Inspecting the prototype-to-concept table does not verify the complete concept predictor. Prototype selection is performed through a learned encoder and latent dot-product similarity, so the model can select prototypes using imperceptible or spurious cues even when the displayed prototype looks appropriate. Likewise, the segmenter observes the image before masking, and mask shapes can transmit information. Consequently, the claimed guarantee that masked features were not used, and the interpretation of latent similarity as “looks like,” are not established.

The formal objective and described implementation appear inconsistent. In the ELBO, the task term is p(y|{c_i}) with observed ground-truth concepts and is therefore independent of the selector and concept decoder. Appendix A instead says that the task predictor receives thresholded predicted concepts. If the latter is used during training, the stated loss is not the derived ELBO; if the former is used, task supervision cannot train the concept pathway. The aggregation of per-part concepts into the task input is also unspecified. Appendix A.2 additionally describes comparing f_concept(e_j) with f_enc(x_i), which generally inhabit different spaces and conflicts with the earlier re-encoding construction.

The accuracy evidence does not support the repeated claim that PGCM matches state-of-the-art CBMs. On CelebA, PGCM has 78.5±0.1 concept accuracy versus 81.3±0.4 for CBM and 83.0±0.0 task accuracy versus 84.0±0.3 for CBM and 84.7±0.5 for CMR. ColorMNIST+ is nearly saturated, while CLEVR-Hans provides only a prototype-count curve and no baseline comparison. Thus the broader performance claim rests on one easy dataset and an underreported evaluation.

The comparisons are not well controlled for the additional localization supervision. PGCM uses supplied masks on CelebA and ColorMNIST+ and SAM with bounding-box prompts on CLEVR-Hans, whereas the baselines operate on full images. The source of CLEVR-Hans boxes at test time is not explained. No prototype-based or concept-grounding baseline is evaluated, despite these being the closest methods to the proposed contribution.

The intervention experiments are insufficiently specified and weakly connected to practical usefulness. The paper does not explain how erroneous prototypes are identified without oracle knowledge, how many are edited or removed, how overrides are implemented, or how much human effort is required. It reports only post-intervention concept accuracy, not downstream task accuracy, and includes no matched editing baseline. PGCM* is worse on CelebA, limiting the generality of the claimed intervenability advantage.

Reproducibility is inadequate. Important details are absent, including dataset sizes and splits, layer widths, embedding dimensions, batch size, epoch count, loss weights, Gaussian variance, preprocessing and augmentation, thresholds, segmentation training details, prototype-editing algorithms, and complete per-dataset results. No code or configuration release is identified. Three seeds do not compensate for these omissions.

Originality is moderate rather than exceptional: the primary construction combines CBMs, part-prototype models, supervised segmentation, and prototype projection/swapping. The manuscript's claims that the limitation is previously unaddressed and that alignment is “resolved” are substantially stronger than the evidence and related-work comparison justify.

There is no dedicated limitations or ethics discussion. This is especially concerning because CelebA experiments predict socially sensitive and subjective facial attributes such as “Male” and “Attractive,” yet demographic bias and misuse are not considered. Swapping prototypes to actual training patches also raises privacy and memorization concerns—particularly for faces—that are not discussed. Dependence on masks, bounding boxes, fixed part decompositions, and extensive human inspection should also be treated as material limitations.

strengths: Originality/significance: Grounding supervised concepts in inspectable image-part prototypes is a useful synthesis of concept bottlenecks and prototype networks. The concept-alignment table and prototype-level editing interface could support more actionable model auditing.

Soundness: The architecture preserves a hard concept bottleneck, uses real training regions after prototype swapping, and evaluates three visually distinct datasets. The noisy-label experiment provides encouraging evidence that prototype editing can improve concept accuracy.
Presentation: The motivation, graphical model, inference pipeline, and qualitative examples are generally clear. The paper also candidly identifies the capacity-versus-cognitive-load tradeoff.
The main predictive comparison covers three seeds and reports both concept and task accuracy. PGCM is competitive on ColorMNIST+ despite its additional structural constraint.
weaknesses: Soundness: The central claim that users can verify alignment is not adequately evaluated. A few author-selected qualitative examples do not establish that humans can reliably detect misalignment across 30–120 prototypes; there is no user study, quantitative alignment metric, systematic prototype audit, or comparison against alternative visualization methods.

The displayed prototype is causally involved in concept prediction, but latent dot-product similarity need not correspond to human visual similarity. Thus the table reveals the model's prototype association without fully guaranteeing that it is faithful evidence for why an input was matched to that prototype. Claims such as replacing an alignment assumption with a 'verifiable mechanism' are consequently too strong.

The formal and implemented training descriptions appear inconsistent. Equation 2 trains p(y|{c_i}) on observed concepts, whereas Appendix A says the task predictor receives thresholded predicted concepts. Hard thresholding also obscures gradient flow. The manuscript must state precisely which quantities are used during training and how the task component is optimized.

The intervention evaluation is weak. Figure 4 reports concept accuracy after oracle concept corrections, rather than downstream task accuracy, so improvement is partly mechanical. PGCM* helps on ColorMNIST+ but is worse than ordinary interventions on CelebA. The model-editing study does not specify the prototype-identification protocol or human effort, compare against CBM editing/retraining, or report task accuracy after editing.

The claim of matching state-of-the-art CBMs is overstated on CelebA: PGCM obtains 78.5 concept accuracy and 83.0 task accuracy versus CBM's 81.3 and 84.0, with reported variation much smaller than the gaps. CLEVR-Hans lacks baseline comparisons, and no statistical tests are provided.

Reproducibility is inadequate without code and several essential details: batch size, epoch count, architecture dimensions, ELBO-term weights, variance/temperature settings, exact aggregation across parts, preprocessing, and full dataset splits. Appendix A.2 also describes a dot product between f_concept(e_j) and f_enc(x_i), which generally have incompatible dimensions and conflicts with the earlier re-encoding description.

Presentation has important ambiguities: CelebA versus CelebA-HQ naming is inconsistent; the construction and aggregation of part-specific labels are underspecified; and SAM is prompted with bounding boxes without clarifying whether these are ground-truth annotations. Adding and relabeling prototypes is described conceptually but not comprehensively evaluated.

Ethics and limitations are insufficiently treated. Experiments predict 'Male,' 'Attractive,' and 'Young' from celebrity faces, yet the paper does not discuss binary/subjective labels, demographic bias, privacy, or risks of deploying visually persuasive but imperfect explanations. Overall, the idea is promising, but the central interpretability evidence and technical specification need substantial strengthening before others can reliably build on it.

strengths: Originality/significance: Grounding supervised concepts in concrete training-image prototypes and exposing a concept-alignment table is a promising synthesis of concept bottlenecks and prototype models. Prototype-level editing could become a useful form of model debugging.

Soundness: The architecture is reasonably well motivated, the probabilistic formulation and ELBO derivation are mostly clear, and the use of re-encoded prototype images attempts to tie predictions to inspectable evidence.

Evaluation: Experiments span four datasets and several segmentation regimes. PGCM remains competitive with CBMs on ColorMNIST+ and CUB, while the capacity study clearly illustrates the prototype-count trade-off.

Presentation/limitations: The paper is generally clear and visually polished. It candidly acknowledges capacity versus cognitive load, dependence on segmentation, and the risk that joint-concept interventions can inadvertently alter other concepts.
weaknesses: Soundness: The central claim of verifiable concept alignment is not demonstrated. Tables 1–2 provide a few selected examples, but there is no human study, exhaustive audit, prototype-purity metric, or comparison measuring whether users can actually detect misalignment. With 120–350 prototypes, practical verification is especially uncertain.

Soundness: The claimed semantics in Eq. 4 do not faithfully describe the implemented predictor. Predictions use soft assignments under a learned dot-product/cosine similarity and weighted concept probabilities before thresholding, rather than an explicit disjunction of prototypes that are 'similar enough.' The learned encoder and similarity function remain opaque, so displaying a selected prototype does not establish that the input and prototype match for a human-recognizable reason.

Evaluation: The editing experiment assumes access to 'wrong prototypes' and their correct labels, but does not specify a reproducible identification protocol, human annotation process, intervention budget, or whether any evaluation labels inform the edits. PGCM* interventions also remove multiple prototype assignments and can change several concepts from one oracle correction, making comparison by number of concept interventions unequal to standard CBM interventions.

Evaluation: Predictive comparisons are confounded by PGCM's segmentation or mask supervision, while baselines apparently operate on full inputs; CLEVR-Hans baselines are omitted. Results use only three seeds without significance testing, and CelebA shows a meaningful concept-accuracy decrease despite the broad claim of similar performance.

Reproducibility/presentation: The code statement has no URL, and essential details are missing, including loss-term weights, most dataset-specific training schedules and architectures, preprocessing and splits, Gaussian variance, prototype-editing rules, and complete segmentation procedures. The paper is therefore not presently sufficient for reliable reproduction.

Significance/ethics: Several proposed capabilities, especially adding prototypes and human correction, are asserted without evaluation. The ethics discussion is generic and does not address the use of CelebA's subjective and sensitive facial attributes ('Attractive,' 'Male,' and 'Young'), demographic bias, consent/privacy, or subgroup performance, despite suggesting possible high-stakes deployment. Overall, the idea has merit, but unsupported central interpretability claims and substantial evaluation and reproducibility gaps prevent acceptance.

strengths: The paper identifies a real weakness of concept bottleneck models: accurate concept labels alone do not establish that the image-to-concept predictor uses the intended visual evidence.

Associating concepts with concrete training-image prototypes is intuitive and potentially useful for inspection and model editing. The concept-alignment table and qualitative visualizations communicate this idea clearly.

PGCM is evaluated on four datasets spanning faces, digits, birds, and synthetic scenes. On the three datasets with baseline comparisons, its task accuracy is broadly competitive with standard concept-based models, and the noisy-label experiment suggests that prototype-level editing can recover some performance.

The manuscript is generally readable, includes an explicit probabilistic formulation and loss derivation, reports results over three seeds for the main accuracy table, and honestly acknowledges capacity–interpretability, segmentation-quality, and intervention-coupling limitations.
weaknesses: Soundness: the central claim of “verifiable concept alignment” is not convincingly evaluated. The paper asks whether humans can verify alignment, but conducts no user study, measures neither verification accuracy nor effort, and provides only a few author-selected prototype examples. Inspecting a prototype image does not establish that the learned selector matches inputs for human-relevant reasons; its encoder and similarity function may still exploit imperceptible or spurious features. Thus the proposed display supplies evidence for inspection, but not the claimed verification guarantee.

The claimed guarantee that re-encoding a prototype image prevents its embedding from containing information absent from that image is largely vacuous: any deterministic image encoder has that property, while it can still encode spurious or non-human-interpretable pixel information. Likewise, masking an input region shows which pixels were available, not which visual property caused the prediction.

The mathematical description and implementation are insufficiently aligned. The ELBO trains the task term using observed concepts, whereas inference uses predicted, thresholded concepts; the manuscript does not clearly explain whether or how the task loss trains the concept pathway. It also alternates between per-part concepts, sets of concepts, and “aggregated” concepts without defining the aggregation, ordering, or matching procedure. These omissions make it difficult to determine exactly what model was evaluated.

The prototype-swapping procedure is inconsistent or underspecified across the main text and appendix. The main text describes decoding and re-encoding learned embeddings, while the appendix replaces them halfway through training with nearest training regions, freezes the images, and discards the original embeddings. How reconstruction, concept relabeling, prototype addition/removal, normalization, and continued optimization work after this operation is not fully specified.

The intervention evidence is weak. Table 4 appears to use oracle knowledge to identify wrong prototypes, but does not specify the selection protocol, number of edited/removed prototypes, human effort, or comparison against plausible CBM repair baselines. Several advertised operations, especially adding prototypes and directly relabeling decoder outputs, are not experimentally demonstrated. Random concept-intervention curves mainly show the expected benefit of overwriting predictions with ground truth and do not establish practical intervention quality.

Experimental controls are incomplete. There are no ablations isolating segmentation, reconstruction, re-encoding, swapping, or concept supervision; no systematic alignment, spurious-correlation, distribution-shift, or failure-case evaluation; and only one prototype-count study. CLEVR-Hans lacks baseline comparisons, and SAM is prompted with bounding boxes whose source and test-time availability are not explained. For CUB, all methods consume embeddings from a ResNet already trained on both class and concept labels, weakening the claim that PGCM itself learns transparent visual grounding.

Originality and significance are overstated. The paper calls concept grounding previously unaddressed while citing visually grounded, locality-aware, and object-centric concept models, but it neither compares empirically against these closest methods nor sharply establishes what capability is unique beyond combining stored visual prototypes with supervised concepts. Tables containing 120 or 350 prototypes may also impose substantial cognitive burden, yet full-table verification cost is not studied.

Reproducibility is inadequate for acceptance. The promised code link is blank, and important details are missing, including network dimensions, dataset splits and preprocessing, loss weights and fixed variance, epoch counts, segmentation training settings, prototype-selection criteria, aggregation rules, noisy CLEVR construction, and exact editing procedures.

Presentation is polished at a high level, but important claims are stated too categorically (“guarantee,” “resolve,” and “verifiable”) relative to the evidence. Some prototype visualizations are tiny, only favorable examples are presented, and the lack of systematic failure analysis makes the qualitative results difficult to assess.

The ethics discussion is too generic given the use of CelebA attributes such as “Attractive,” “Male,” and “Young,” and the paper’s suggested high-stakes applications. It does not discuss demographic bias, binary gender labeling, privacy or consent concerns, or the risks of treating prototype inspection as assurance of safety. Dataset licenses are listed, but compliance with CelebA’s non-commercial restriction is not discussed.

strengths: Significance/originality: Grounding supervised CBM concepts in concrete training-set image parts is a useful synthesis of concept bottlenecks and prototype models. The concept-alignment table is intuitive, and prototype-level editing is a practically interesting interaction mechanism.

Soundness: The evaluation covers four substantially different datasets, three seeds, several CBM baselines, multiple segmentation regimes, capacity sensitivity, concept/task interventions, and controlled label corruption. PGCM matches CBM performance on ColorMNIST+ and CUB, with only a moderate reduction on CelebA.

The noisy-label experiment provides encouraging evidence for editability: correcting or removing erroneous prototypes raises concept accuracy from 92.8–92.9% to 96.9–97.8% on ColorMNIST+ and from 81.6% to 95.1–97.5% on CLEVR-Hans3.

Presentation: The motivation, architecture, prototype-swapping mechanism, and qualitative examples are generally clear. The paper also honestly discusses the capacity–interpretability trade-off, segmentation dependence, and possible harmful intervention effects.

Reproducibility/ethics: The appendix reports seeds, hardware, approximate runtimes, optimizers, prototype counts, and major architectural choices. Dataset licenses and the non-commercial restriction of CelebA are acknowledged.
weaknesses: Soundness: The central claim of “verifiable concept alignment” is not convincingly evaluated. Evidence consists mainly of a few author-selected prototype examples from one seed; there is no user study, systematic alignment/purity metric, failure-case audit, or measurement of whether humans can inspect 120 CelebA or 350 CUB prototypes reliably. Predictive accuracy does not validate interpretability or semantic alignment.

The asserted semantics do not appear to match the implemented inference exactly. Equation 4 describes a concept as an existential disjunction over sufficiently similar prototypes, whereas Equation 2 predicts it by thresholding an expectation under a soft categorical distribution. Mixtures of several prototypes can therefore activate a concept even when no individual prototype satisfies the stated condition.

The training account is internally unclear. In the presented ELBO, the task term p(y|{c_i}) conditions on observed concepts and does not train the input-to-concept path, while the implementation describes feeding thresholded predicted concepts to the task predictor. Hard thresholding is non-differentiable, and the manuscript does not explain how this implemented task loss corresponds to the derived objective.

The “hard guarantee” that prototypes encode only inspectable information is overstated. Re-encoding a displayed training patch through a black-box encoder does not ensure that similarity decisions use human-recognizable features, nor does inspecting a prototype establish faithfulness of the selector. Imperceptible or incidental cues within the patch can still drive selection.

The editing experiment assumes erroneous prototypes can be identified and corrected, apparently with oracle knowledge of the synthetically corrupted labels. It does not measure human identification accuracy, editing effort, collateral effects, or the proposed addition of new prototypes, so it only partially supports the intervention claims.

Reproducibility is incomplete: the displayed code-availability statement has no URL, loss weights and detailed layer configurations are omitted, dataset splits and several preprocessing choices are underspecified, and the appendix explains ColorMNIST+ label corruption but not the corresponding CLEVR-Hans3 corruption procedure. The source of the bounding-box prompts used with SAM is also unclear.

Originality is somewhat constrained by closely related visually grounded and locality-aware CBM work cited by the paper. The empirical comparison excludes these closest approaches and all baselines on CLEVR-Hans3, making it difficult to establish the incremental benefit of explicit decoded/training-instance prototypes.

Overall, the core idea is promising and the predictive results are respectable, but unsupported interpretability claims, the mismatch between formal semantics and inference, and missing experimental/reproducibility details prevent others from reliably validating the main contribution. These issues outweigh the merits in the current version.
